parts.display_text:
An isotope has half-life 28 hours. What is the approximate probability that a particular undecayed nucleus decays during the next 1.0 second?

A. 1/(28 ln 2)
B. 1/(28×3600×ln 2)
C. ln 2/(28×3600)
D. ln 2/28

answer.text: C. The decay constant in s⁻¹ is λ=ln 2/(28×3600). For a 1s interval much shorter than the half-life, probability≈λΔt, giving the expression in C, about 6.88×10⁻⁶.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Nuclide X decays to stable Y. The source graph shows their numbers crossing at time s. If X has decay constant λ, what is s? A. ln 2/λ  B. 1/λ  C. λ/ln 2  D. ln 2

answer.text: Official answer A; editorial worked explanation: If initially all nuclei are X, then N_X = N₀e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃᵗ and N_Y = N₀−N_X. At the crossing, N_X=N_Y=N₀/2. Thus e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃˢ=1/2 and s=ln 2/λ, the half-life.
answer.evidence: Official May 2023 Physics HL Paper 1 TZ1 answer grid checked on PDF page 3; explanation independently calculated from the visible source question.

answer.text:
Official answer C checked; editorial worked explanation:

A proton-rich nuclide can move toward stability by converting a proton into a neutron. Beta-plus decay performs this conversion while leaving nucleon number unchanged. Therefore C.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Sometimes the alpha decay of thorium is accompanied by gamma-ray emission. Suggest an explanation.

answer.text: Official markscheme explanation; editorial worked explanation: The alpha decay can leave the daughter radium nucleus in an excited discrete nuclear energy level. The radium nucleus then moves to a lower nuclear energy level and emits the energy difference as a gamma-ray photon.
answer.evidence: Official May 2024 Physics HL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6708M checked on PDF page(s) 13; editorial explanation independently recalculated against the source task.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: In beta-minus decay, electrons are emitted with a continuous range of kinetic energies up to an endpoint. Explain why this led to the proposal of another emitted particle.

answer.text: For a fixed nuclear transition the available energy is fixed, but the beta electron does not always carry the same energy. Another particle can carry the varying remainder while conserving energy and momentum. In β⁻ decay this particle is an electron antineutrino; the daughter nucleus also recoils.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A closed rock sample originally contained rubidium-87 and no strontium-87. All strontium-87 now present was produced by rubidium decay, and no parent or daughter atoms have entered or left. The sample now has 2.232 mg of rubidium-87 and 0.028 mg of strontium-87. Take their atomic masses as equal for this estimate and λ=4.50×10⁻¹⁹ s⁻¹. Determine the rock’s age in years; use 1 year=3.156×10⁷ s.

answer.text: The initial parent number equals the surviving parent plus daughter numbers. With equal atomic masses, N₀/N=(2.232+0.028)/2.232=2.26/2.232. From N=N₀e⁻λᵗ, t=ln(N₀/N)/λ≈2.77×10¹⁶ s≈8.78×10⁸ years.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: The graph shows binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number A. Identify the broad feature that supports the short range of the strong nuclear force, and relate it to the nucleons with which each nucleon interacts.

answer.text: Above about A=60 the binding energy per nucleon stays approximately constant, with a gradual decline, rather than growing in proportion to A. This supports a short-range force: each nucleon binds mainly with a limited number of nearby nucleons rather than with every nucleon in the nucleus.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Xenon-132 is stable whereas xenon-142 is unstable. Both have proton number 54. Suggest why xenon-142 is unstable.

answer.text: It has too many neutrons for its proton number: its neutron-to-proton ratio lies above the stable range.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A radioactive sample has decay constant λ and initially contains N₀ nuclei at time zero. It contains N₁ undecayed nuclei at time t₁ and N₂ at a later time t₂. Which expression is correct?

A. N₂ = N₁ exp[−λ(t₂ − t₁)]
B. N₂ = N₁ exp[−λ(t₂ + t₁)]
C. N₂ = (N₁/N₀) exp[−λ(t₂ − t₁)]
D. N₂ = (N₁/N₀) exp[−λ(t₂ + t₁)]

answer.text: A. Apply exponential decay over the elapsed time t₂ − t₁, using N₁ as the population at the start of that interval.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Two initially pure radioactive samples X and Y decay directly to stable products. The graph shows their activities in units of A against time in units of T. Their initial activities are 4A and A respectively.

(a) For each sample, determine its half-life and express its decay constant and initial number of radioactive nuclei using A and T.
(b) Determine when their activities become equal, in units of T.

answer.text:
(a) X has half-life 2T, decay constant λ_X = ln 2/(2T), and N_X0 = 4A/λ_X = 8AT/ln 2. Y has half-life 3T, λ_Y = ln 2/(3T), and N_Y0 = A/λ_Y = 3AT/ln 2.
(b) Set 4A exp[−t ln 2/(2T)] = A exp[−t ln 2/(3T)]. Then ln 4 = t ln 2/(6T), giving t = 12T.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A sample initially contains N₀ radioactive nuclei. The graph shows ln(N/N₀) against time t, with t in milliseconds.

(a) Name the quantity equal to the magnitude of the gradient.
(b) Determine the half-life in milliseconds.

answer.text:
(a) From N = N₀e^(−λt), ln(N/N₀) = −λt, so the gradient magnitude is the decay constant λ.
(b) The line reaches −1.4 at about 0.84 ms, giving λ = 1.4/0.84 = 1.67 ms⁻¹. Half-life is ln 2/λ = 0.416 ms ≈ 0.42 ms.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
In β⁻ decay, each nucleus releases the same total energy, but emitted β⁻ particles have a continuous range of kinetic energies. What explains this?

A. Energy is given to remaining nucleons
B. Energy is taken by an emitted antineutrino
C. Energy is used to create the β⁻ particle
D. Energy is used to create a new nucleon

answer.text:
Official key B checked; editorial worked explanation:

B. Beta decay is a three-body process involving the daughter nucleus, electron and antineutrino. The fixed decay energy is shared in varying proportions, so the electron has a continuous kinetic-energy range while the antineutrino carries the complementary amount.

evidence.detail: Cambridge 9702/11 May/June 2024 published markscheme, PDF page 3, key B; explanation authored and checked against the complete source question.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Which statement about radioactive decay is correct?

A. Neutrinos are always emitted in α decay.
B. α particles have a continuous kinetic-energy range.
C. β⁻ particles have a continuous kinetic-energy range.
D. Proton number decreases by four in α decay.

answer.text:
Official key C checked; editorial worked explanation:

C. Beta decay shares a fixed decay energy among the daughter nucleus, beta particle and neutrino or antineutrino, so beta particles have a continuous kinetic-energy spectrum. Alpha particles from a specific transition have discrete energies, and alpha decay lowers proton number by two.

evidence.detail: Cambridge 9702/12 May/June 2024 published key C, PDF page 3; explanation is editorial.
